endorsements.quote: To mitigate these risks, AI systems should complement rather than replace human expertise.

The broad distribution of such images for clinical, research, or training purposes necessitates explicit patient consent and anonymization to safeguard individuals’ privacy and avoid unethically publicizing sensitive images.
Even trained on extensive datasets, AI tools remain susceptible to the effects of data imbalance, necessitating meticulously curated, representative datasets to mitigate biased outcomes.

Well-defined frameworks are essential to delineate the responsibilities of health professionals, AI designers, and healthcare institutions, encompassing validation of AI outputs, mitigation of algorithmic bias, risk management, and continuous monitoring to uphold patient safety and care quality.
Clear and interpretable AI outputs are essential to support informed clinical decision-making and uphold patient autonomy.

unlisted_practices: Use primary patient datasets and secondary metadata only with proper authorization.
Use standardized validation frameworks and prospective multi-tiered testing to confirm algorithmic reliability and generalizability in real-world clinical contexts.
Provide professional training and AI literacy to imaging professionals to mitigate overreliance.
